Pharpar
FAR-par
proper noun
One of the two rivers of Damascus, named by Naaman the Syrian leper when he despised the prophet’s command to wash in Jordan; the name is taken to mean “swift” or “rushing.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Pharpar was one of the two rivers of Damascus, named in the account of Naaman the Syrian leper. When the prophet Elisha bade him go wash seven times in the Jordan and be clean, Naaman was wroth, both at the plainness of the cure and at the choice of so mean a river: “Are not Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? may I not wash in them, and be clean?” (2Ki 5:12). To his proud eye, the clear rivers of his own city were nobler than the muddy Jordan, and the whole business beneath his dignity. So he turned away in a rage, and would have gone home a leper still, but that his servants reasoned him into obedience: if the prophet had bidden some great thing, would he not have done it? how much rather, then, wash and be clean. He humbled himself, went down into the despised Jordan, and came up whole. The river Pharpar stands for the pride that despises God’s appointed way of cleansing and prefers its own. Men still say, in effect, Are not the waters of my own choosing better? — preferring their own works, their own reason, their own religion to the one simple, humbling way God has set. But there is cleansing in no river but the one God appoints; the leprosy of sin is washed away only in the blood of Christ, and only by those who will stoop to the humbling gospel and obey.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A river of Damascus named by proud Naaman, who despised washing in Jordan; a rebuke to the pride that prefers its own way of cleansing to God’s appointed one.

PHARPAR, one of the two rivers of Damascus.

Naaman named it when he despised washing in Jordan (2Ki 5:12).

The name is taken to mean swift, or rushing.

To his pride, the rivers of Damascus seemed nobler than Jordan.

It rebukes the pride that prefers its own way of cleansing to God’s.

📖 Key Scripture

2Ki 5:12 — "Are not Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? may I not wash in them, and be clean? So he turned and went away in a rage."

2Ki 5:13 — "And his servants came near, and spake unto him, and said, My father, if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing, wouldest thou not have done it? how much rather then, when he saith to thee, Wash, and be clean?"

2Ki 5:14 — "Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God: and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean."

Pro 14:12 — "There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A river of Scripture named by proud Naaman; it rebukes the pride that prefers its own way of cleansing to the simple, humbling way God has appointed.

expand to see more

Pharpar names a live and abiding corruption: the pride that despises God’s appointed way of salvation and prefers its own. As Naaman esteemed the rivers of Damascus above the muddy Jordan, so men still prefer their own works, their own reason, their own religion to the one simple, humbling gospel, saying, Are not the waters of my own choosing better?

Scripture answers that there is cleansing in no river but the one God appoints. “There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death” (Pro 14:12). The leprosy of sin is washed away only in the blood of Christ, and only by those who will stoop to obey the humbling word. Naaman went down into the despised Jordan and came up clean; the proud who will not stoop go home defiled.
